Technically what you're talking about already exists (See the International Space Station), but it has a whole host of sustainability problems. Even if we got all of the things you mentioned up into orbit, there's still a really big (basically unsolvable from orbit) problem - sustainable radiation shielding. We kind of take that for granted here on Earth, as our atmosphere does it for us, but that's not the case when we leave the protective confines. While this isn't a problem for anything that we fabricate on Earth and send up (anything being launched is horrifically expensive), this becomes a huge problem if we ever want to expand the things we have in place that are already up there or on another planet (Although, on another planet we'd probably be focused on terraforming it so that it has an atmosphere to protect us, like Earth does. Alternatively, we'd have to figure out how to fabricate shielding from the available materials there).

Further, micrometeroid weathering means that eventually the shielding elements will need to be replaced (we don't have a good solution for this). So, if you're talking about "Why don't we have a large scale space colony in orbit", the answer is because we don't have answers for a sustainable orbital habitat. If you're talking about why we don't have one on another planet, getting the necessary stuff there and then figuring out how to deal with adjusting to the specific challenges of the planet are pretty difficult.

Terraforming proposals for either Mars or Venus usually seems to involving millions or some other astronomical number of tons of material to the planet, something I don't think will be possible for hundreds of years, if not ever possible.

But, when you think about it, a lot of problems that a giant space station in orbit might have, actually have solutions on Mars. Radiation and meteorites?, we could potentially build a colony with plenty of radiation protection on the surface if you take enough material there, or just use the surface as a radiation shield and live a couple meters below ground the majority of the time. Water has been shown to be incredibly abundant on Mars, so if you land a few nuclear reactors and that would provide the oxygen, energy and drinking water you need. From there it will be a quest of trying to find resources on mars so that the colony can best use the resources that don't need to be shipped from Earth.

Any colony on Mars will be incredibly difficult to set up, but it definitely seems that the most basic needs of a colony (water, air, and energy) can be provided with technology that's already well developed (nuclear submarines kind of being the guide to this). Of course this will take hundreds of launches, and if this is far enough in the future, I suspect the majority of the colony's construction might be done with drones and the vast majority of colonists arriving until only after completion.

Within the next 50 years, we will have small settlements on another planet. However, an entire colony or civilization on another planet won't come for another 100 or so years.

Our main issue is time. It takes way too long to transport people and/or goods to another planet. Once we accomplish a form of travel that makes time much more simplified, then we will see a gigantic boom in colonization on other planets.

Lastly, NASA is no longer relevant in space anymore. When I was at Stennis a couple months ago, we took a look at the new SLS, which is their only objective at this time. Space exploration is being pushed to the private sector and eventually NASA will be obsolete and/or shift their priorities to deep exploration and nothing more.

The real question is, why would you build a colony in the middle of space?

Colonisation only happens when there is an economic or strategic reason to do so. Space is little more than a vacuum: you can't really mine anything from it, you can't farm in it cheaper than you can farm the same things on earth, and there isn't anything you can only build in zero gravity that you can't build for less on Earth. There isn't really any whole or large branch of science you need people in space to do -- radio astronomy can be done by remote from telescopes -- and we've reached a point in automation where it isn't necessary to put a flight of Space Marines in orbital bases, robots and satellites can shoot missiles down just as easily.

What you need to have space colonies is: something you can do in space that can't be done cheaper or for just as much on Earth ... or indeed that can't be done cheaper with a colony on Mars or the Moon.
